title: #307 | Cronicamente offline
description: nas edições anteriores #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 “A habilidade mais importante do próximo século não vai ser conectar humanos com mais tecnologia. Vai ser conectar humanos uns com os outros”. _ “Ninguém confia no gosto de quem só consome fast-food”. _ Em 2025, a WGSN já tinha previsto que a fadiga digital e o excesso de estímulos levaria as pessoas a migrarem para comunidades no mundo real: “Até 2027, a busca por menos barulho e mais desconexão digital vai ser o novo normal, emergindo como uma demonstração de autocuidado em forma de ambientes mais calmos, seguros e significativos” Isso tem se traduzido na realização e/ou incentivo de todo tipo de experiência. Um grande destaque no Brasil, que ilustra tanto o pertencimento quanto o autocuidado e, claro, a presença das marcas, são as corridas de rua. Segundo a Exame , em 2024 foram realizadas 2.827 corridas de rua oficiais no país. Em 2025, mais de 5 mil. Além disso, temos visto o crescimento de eventos em lojas, jantares especiais para clientes, clubes do livro, exibições em salas de cinema e convites para as mais diversas atividades físicas, manuais, intelectuais e sociais. E assim seguirá essa tendência - em 2027 e além. O que nos traz à edição de hoje é a sua relação com a creator economy . No que o Digiday chamou de “ vibes over metrics ”, os eventos presenciais agora são também uma estratégia de engajamento e construção de comunidade para marcas pessoais - ou marcas essencialmente virtuais. _ Três movimentos estão por trás disso: 1 - O mundo “pós-feed”, em que as redes sociais se tornaram oficialmente plataformas de descoberta e entretenimento, e onde “número de seguidores” é uma métrica cada vez menos determinante de sucesso e engajamento. Hoje, a viralização está muito mais ligada à adequação de um conteúdo a um nicho, assunto, tom ou formato (ou todos ao mesmo tempo). Mas quando encontrar uma audiência tem se tornado mais fácil, aprofundar essa relação é o desafio. Seja criando um universo de marca que gere reconhecimento e lembrança, seja reunindo essas pessoas para além do feed. 2 - A busca por mais presença , que é comum a todas as gerações e todos os nichos - todo mundo gostaria de ter mais atenção, mais concentração e mais serendipidade na vida. O que varia muito é como isso acontece. Quais rituais alguém pode incorporar ao seu dia a dia? Qual a periodicidade ideal desses encontros? Qual a atmosfera perfeita para proporcionar aquilo que alguém mais precisa? Assim como fazem com o seu conteúdo, seja lifestyle, seja desenvolvimento profissional, a curadoria e capacidade de simplificar informações dos creators tem muito valor aqui. O que nos traz ao próximo ponto. 3 - O tal do repertório, que nunca se falou tanto em construir, mas que não está nos mesmos vídeos ou carrosseis virais que todo mundo está compartilhando. Repertório é o que se traduz em uma perspectiva única que só aquela pessoa consegue trazer, com base em tudo que ela carrega consigo. Textos, imagens, experiências, tudo aquilo que você já viu e vivenciou, o lugar da onde você vem, os lugares por onde já passou, as boas conversas, os livros fáceis ou difíceis, os hábitos diários e ambientes que frequenta… Tudo isso forma o seu repertório. Que pode ser composto, sim, pelo que passa pelo feed e vai morar na sua pasta de “salvos” ou no mosaico mental de referências que você acessa a cada job. Mas um ponto de vista realmente original não vem de consumir mais do mesmo, ou apenas o que é filtrado por algoritmos. Vem de uma vida interessante o suficiente para influenciar tudo que você faz. Uma vida que acontece através de telas, mas principalmente fora delas. Naqueles ambientes em que conseguimos estar presentes com todo o nosso corpo (não apenas os nossos dedos em contato com uma tela fria). Naqueles momentos em que uma informação é registrada não porque é vista, mas porque é vivida, com todas as nuances do ambiente, das pessoas que estão ali e de como ela é apresentada. No conhecimento que alguém realmente tem para passar - sem ferramentas que escrevem roteiros, sem a chance de regravar até ficar bom o suficiente. Nas trocas que a gente não consegue pensar antes de digitar ou gravar duas ou três vezes antes de enviar. Depois de anos cronicamente online, é por essas e outras que o conteúdo, a influência e as comunidades têm buscado o offline. _ Quando “comunidade” era a grande tendência nos relatórios, a gente se tornava uma. Quando carrosséis anunciavam o retorno das revistas impressas, a nossa já estava na gráfica. Quando certos produtos físicos estavam virando colecionáveis, o nosso boné esgotou em 24 horas. Agora, chegou a vez da gente olhar para o offline - como movimento de mercado e necessidade humana - do único jeito que a gente sabe fazer: ✨ na prática ✨ Topam ser uma comunidade presencial também? :) Nosso encontro está marcado no dia 27 de outubro, terça-feira, na Avenida Paulista. title: The 5 big lessons designers must learn
description: Much of my work here has been about teaching important truths that are overlooked in design school and culture. As we head into the fall it’s a good time to revisit the 5 most important lessons for all designers to learn. Here they are: Someone has to pay. No matter how great your idea is, someone has to pay for it. Are you paying? Probably not. This means your idea depends on getting someone else to put their money behind your idea. To build something you think is high quality probably means better planning, bigger budgets, smarter leaders or healthier teams, all of which someone has to pay for. Designers are trained to care first about craft and quality, but without convincing someone to pay for it those things can not happen. Most people, most of the time, need to be convinced to spend more. Quality is easier to sell to people. If you are trying to make better design happen it’s more effective to use the word quality . This is a word most people understand and care about. But design is a term few people understand and it has a superficial baggage to it like style fads do. When we talk about “good design” we really mean “a higher quality” product or service and it’s easier to get what you want from people if use the language of quality that they use (e.g. higher profits or customer satisfaction). The powerful decide. Do you decide the budget, schedule or goals for the projects you work on? Whoever does is the real decision-maker and designer of the project. Designers are often advisers more than deciders. This means the less power you have, the more you must use influence and trusted relationships to get your ideas out into the world. Design is decided by power and influence more than talent. These are learnable skills critical to fulfilling creative careers. Good depends on the context. What is the best car? Or hammer? We can’t answer without a context. Is the car for street racing or to take kids to soccer practice? Designers rush to opinions about “good” based on their own preferences. In the real world the most critical design goal is affordability , as people can not buy a design they can not afford. Often the biggest design constraint is bureaucracy , which even a genius designer could not overcome without learning how to earn trust and to use organizations to their advantage . Without knowing the context and constraints a designer faced we can’t really judge the work we see. Design for sale vs. Design for use. People often purchase products before they get to try them. This means products are often designed primarily to be sold, rather than for their UX. A classic example is a microwave or washing machine with 50 buttons on the front. It’s easy to believe, as a consumer, that more features is higher quality. This is design for sale . Yet we know for UX, less, but better designed, features is higher quality. This mismatch explains why low quality UX is pervasive. The tension in many organizations is between designing for sale and designing for use. If you want to learn to apply these lessons in your work, read my books How Design Makes The World and Why Design Is Hard . Watch the talk: the greatest design lessons You can watch or listen to me presenting these lessons , with lots of fun visual examples including Thor’s hammer Mjölnir, annoying clamshell packaging, rotary phones, IKEA, confusing roads, the planet earth, 747 cockpits and more.

title: #306 | Uma seleção de campanhas
description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Inclusive, fazemos vários. O formato inicialmente permitia compartilhar dez imagens em um único post, e depois foi expandido para vinte. Primeiro, foi utilizado pelos millennials como álbum do Orkut - registros agrupados de um mesmo evento. Depois a gen Z, querendo performar menos, intercalou fotos posadas com fotos aleatórias e chamou de dump . Enquanto isso, a bolha criadora de conteúdo tratava as telas como slides e elaborava apresentações sobre todo tipo de assunto - com call to action no final, claro. Salve, compartilhe, assine, contrate, inscreva-se. O carrossel é um dos formatos preferidos de quem busca engajamento. Basta um questionamento bem amplo e chamativo na capa, seguido por uma série de telas que ora explicam, ora confundem. O resultado é a banalização de questões extremamente profundas - como se a resposta coubesse em um carrossel de Instagram. Ou como se eles fossem de fato lidos com a devida atenção, ou escritos com a pretensão de elaborar uma pauta para além do rage bait da capa. Como se eles fossem sequer escritos por uma outra pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. title: How to reinvent your life
description: Next week is the launch of my tenth book, How To Live Rules For People Who Don’t Like Rules . This Substack has always been free and I hope you’ll check it out. If you’re at a crossroads in life, I wrote it for you! Why? The design world is a crazy place! Yet you are smart and creative. With a little help from the wisest ideas in history, you can sort yourself out more easily than you think. You don’t need a guru or a fancy program: all the secrets are within you. The essay below offers one idea from the book on how to reinvent your life. How to reinvent your life There is a list of sayings on a whiteboard near my desk that I can’t help but notice. It contains ideas I try to remember, things I forget are true and important about the life I want to have. Near the top of the list is this one: you could be dead. It makes me laugh every time I see it, for reasons I can’t entirely explain. When we’ve been alive for decades we forget what being alive means . We slide into a paper cage of our own habits and forget that with a little effort we can slide our way into new habits too. I can stand up whenever I want. Or sit down. Or put on some music, or close my eyes and lose myself in silence. I could dance, scream, stand on my desk, or anything I choose to do. Anyone can do an infinite number of different things, small and large, in this or in any moment as long as they are still alive. But I forget. We all forget. We live many of our waking moments asleep in a lazy dream of our own invention, a dream of boredom and regret that we don’t even enjoy. We become familiar with our favorite memories and allow ourselves to believe the feeling of familiarity is an acceptable replacement for investing in the life we have today. There are hundreds of cliches about how to live life and it’s easy to dismay cliches. Sayings like “Carpe Diem”, “ Memento mori “, or even “Sing like no one is listening” are reminders we often see, inspiring us to nod our heads affirmatively, “Yes! I should be more in the moment!” but then our attention moves on and we return to our waking slumber. We fool ourselves into the confusion that thinking about doing something, thinking about writing a book, thinking about changing a career, is practice for actually doing it. But merely thinking about playing guitar does not make you a better guitar player. How many people do we know who continually talk about the movie they want to make, the company they want to start, or the trip they want to take, yet never take even the smallest act towards that goal? Complacency is a disease of affluence: if our lives were worse perhaps we’d be desperate enough to take chances, since we’d be less afraid of what we have to lose. Children are masters of reinvention. Every day for them is another dream, another game, another world of kings and queens, or dragons and unicorns. Why as adults does it become so scary to try something new? We know our proudest memories involve moments of fear, risk, and doubt that we overcame. All adults remember dozens of firsts, their first time riding a bicycle, their first good grade, their first kiss or midnight tryst, yet along the way into middle age we forget the fear we felt before we did those things. It doesn’t make sense: why do we become more afraid of fear as we age, when we should have more experience with it and how to use it to our advantage? A masterful life would have an increasing number of risks and chances, perhaps carefully considered but risks no less, taken in it, not fewer. Why not try a new philosophy? A new kind of music? A new relationship? The older we are the less there is to lose. Every winter the trees shed their leaves. They bravely drop their finely crafted foliage into the dirt, literally leaving parts of themselves and their past behind, to make room for what’s going to come next. Life itself is a cycle of ending things to start new ones. It’s only the dead rocks and cold stones that move only when pushed. The very cells in your body don’t live forever, they fade away every few weeks to be regenerated and renewed. On each day you are lucky enough to wake up, your body has changed, reinventing itself as a natural course of your biology. It’s stasis that’s unnatural. Staying in the same place, with the same thoughts, the same sadness, takes more energy than moving on. I’m 54 years old. As the darker cliches go I should be stuck in the loops of my memories, telling the same safe stories of past adventures, pretending it feels as good and as real as doing something interesting today. But I’m not. I’m on my second career now, not out of any particular kind of courage but simply because I decided I wanted to live in the present, and not let myself hide in my memories or be a slave to my doubts. Even if I fail to live up to my ambitions, I wake up each day giving myself a chance to discover a new dream, a new possibility, a new chance that, however small, I’d never find if I believed all of my imagined limitations. I’m here! I’m alive! I’m doing this right now! These are things I can say to myself during my days, even if they are the only reward for my efforts. I’m not dead yet and I will treat every day as the precious mystery that it is. Life is to be lived. To try, to reach, to stretch, to dance, and sure, yes, to cry and fail at times, but the avoidance of uncertainty is a denial of life itself. I hope you’ll check out How To Live: Rules For People Who Don’t Like Rules .

description: Hi folks. A break from design this week to help me pay the bills (remember this Substack has always been free!). Here are some early reviews: “This book is full of wisdom and great advice for how to spend your years on earth… your life will be richer for it.” — A.J. Jacobs, bestselling author of The Year of Living Biblically “A thoughtful treatise on living mindfully that combines everyman wisdom with a healthy dose of irreverence.” - Kirkus reviews “I am smitten with How To Live. In just one hour, on the second day of my senior year at Bayside High School in NYC, I broke two. I was a good student, but on that day, still feeling the joys of summer, I forgot to do my physics homework. My teacher, Mr. Sussman, was a bully and had a reputation for making fun of students he didn’t like. I feared teachers like him and tried to stay out of trouble, but on that day something changed. My rules for life were forming, I just didn’t know it yet. Mr. Sussman had the crooked smile of a second-rate FBI interrogator. He wasn’t very tall or athletic, but in moments like this, where he felt that he had an advantage, he’d stalk the front of the classroom like an eager middle-aged chimpanzee. He calmly told me, and two other forgetful students, to stand up. He took his time, with long pauses as he moved around the room, telling jokes about how foolish we were. The class laughed with him. Eventually, he looked at me and asked, almost rhetorically, “How could you possibly forget on the first day?” And then something happened. Without thinking, I spoke up. I replied, “Well, how could you give such a forgettable assignment?” The class laughed and gasped at the same time. They were shocked I did what many wished someone would do. I hadn’t planned it. I guess some part of me decided to defend myself. Mr. Sussman was mortified. He angrily pointed to the door while glaring at me and yelled, “You! To the dean’s office, now!” And I left. Being sent to the dean’s office was the ultimate punishment a teacher could give. But I walked out of the room in frustration more than fear. I didn’t feel good about what I had done, but it didn’t feel bad either. The interesting part of the story, given the goals of this book, is what happened next. The dean’s office was empty so I sat and waited. I’d never been to the dean’s office before and didn’t know what the rules were. They weren’t posted anywhere, so how was I supposed to know them? Soon the class bell rang and an idea came to mind. Could I just leave? The whole idiotic exchange was a waste of time, and if I missed another class I’d have more catching up to do. Wasn’t the ultimate goal here for me to learn? I thought so, and I got up and left. I chose to let the dean, Mr. Sussman, and whoever else was involved in the high school corrections system industrial-complex decide what rules I broke, if any, and what the punishment should be. Can you guess what happened in the end? Nothing. To my surprise, the whole incident never came up again, almost like it never occurred. I discovered that rules are not always what they seem. My goal in this book is to teach you how to live well. Rules are good when they are wise and help us make good decisions. However, we don’t like rules when they are thoughtless, shallow, or serve only the people who enforce them, which is true too often. For this reason, the focus of this book is not the rules of institutions like schools, religions, or societies. Instead, it’s about what you can control: your inner life and your relationship with yourself. I’ve learned that if you only live by your own rules, you live alone. But if you always follow other people’s rules, you never live your own life. So what is the answer then? It comes from finding balance, and I will help you do this. I’ve labeled the advice in this book as rules, because it’s the word that makes the most sense to me, but you could just as well call it wisdom, principles, guidelines, or philosophies. These are not restrictive rules, telling you what you can’t do. Instead, they are empowering tools for living well. Here’s all you need to know about me. I’m 54 years old. I’ve had a great life, far better than I ever dreamed in Mr. Sussman’s class. I’ve spent 20 years traveling the world to talk about ideas from my books, meeting fascinating people and having experiences that opened my mind. I’ll use stories from my life, since I know it better than any other, to give you what the great philosopher Montaigne might call an “honest book.” I am well aware that what worked for me is not guaranteed to help anyone else. With that in mind, I’ve crafted the rules in this book to be as useful as possible for everyone. Part One While I was dying in the ICU of a hospital in Pittsburgh, I was surprised at the noise of the machines that were keeping me alive. Each one had a different yet equally annoying sound. All I wanted to do was rest, but every machine insisted on reminding me incessantly that it was doing its job. BEEP (I am checking if your heart rate is safe). BLOOP WHIRR CLANK (I am transfusing blood for you). There were five of these devices, and I was grateful for all of them, but did they need to be so loud? Each one had a different tone and rhythm, as if some mad genius composer had crafted a symphony for torturing people while they fought for their lives. I tell you this not to complain, I’m grateful for these inventions, but to teach you the first rule of this book. One night, they needed to move my bed to do some tests that would reveal if I was healing. They unplugged many of the machines and moved me into a long, empty hallway to wait for testing. Finally it was quiet and I was alone, free from the endless poking and prodding from doctors, nurses, and family. It was peaceful at first, but soon I realized that without those monitors I could die. I’d lost so much blood and was severely anemic, which meant my heart could fail. And if it did, no one would know and I’d be gone forever. I was young, and one fear led to another. I convinced myself that if I fell asleep, as much as I wanted to, I’d never wake up. I kept my eyes open, fighting through tears to stay alive. I am glad I did not die. And I am glad that you, dear reader, are not dead either. Which leads to the first rule of How to Live. 1. Don’t Die If you think this rule is obvious, you’re mostly right. One way you’re wrong is that most of the universe has broken rule number one. Of all the people, animals, and species who had a chance to live since time began, more than 99.9% of them are currently dead. 150,000 people will die today, more than you could meet in several lifetimes. To all of these dead people and creatures, your existence is a triumph. You have won a great victory in the history of the universe just by being here. Good job. The legendary TV show, The Sopranos , notable for how miserable every character was, popularized a wise observation: “Sometimes I go about in pity for myself, and all the while, a great wind carries me across the sky.” 1 Being alive is our great wind. Any day we wake up and are not dead, or in great pain, is a victory. It seems obvious until we realize that most of our waking hours are spent taking life for granted. You could’ve been born a third-generation slave, tortured and worked to the bone every day of your life. Or watched your young family die of the plague, a terribly painful disease that consumed you last. Humans are a silly species, and our habit of forgetting the most important things is among the silliest. One selfish reason I’m glad you’re not dead is that dead people do not buy books. Dead people do not seem to read well either; they get terrible scores on reading comprehension tests. Writers write for the living because there’s no sense in writing for the dead. The dead are out of chances. If you die midway through this sentence, and break this first rule, I cannot help you. But assuming you are alive, and not just a dead person pretending to be alive to impress your dead friends, you still have chances to turn things around. You never know how many chances you will get, but one can be enough, and my goal in this book is to help you use it. I realize that “don’t die” sounds negative. It could be more positively stated as stay alive, or love life. But describing death as something to avoid makes me laugh, and laughing about death helps me laugh about life. Laughing means your mind is open. We only laugh when we can look at something in more than one way, but too often we get stuck on one narrow perspective. Something bad happens and we cry out, “Why me?” and obsess about our suffering. “Why not me?” is more reasonable to ask because we know everyone gets their turn. There is a reason the Budai, the Laughing Buddha, is always shown having a good time and giving gifts. He knew there’s a way to see the humor in all things, and when we do, life gets better. This is similar to the spirit of the saying “God is a comedian playing to an audience that is too afraid to laugh.” 2 Why fear something, like the unknown, if laughing at it is more helpful? If being afraid benefits you, then, by all means, tremble at your own shadow all day long. But if it makes things worse? Shouldn’t you try something else? Nietzsche wisely advised us to only believe in a god that can dance. 3 Our gods are pictured as miserable, scary, and judgy. But what if they were dancing? It’s harder to judge others while dancing, even if they are bad at it, and this is true for both gods and people. Even Jesus, in his first miracle, made wine from water. I’m sure he was amused when he did it; it’s an act of joyous mischief to save the day at a wedding but keep it a secret. 4 Yet I’ve never seen a painting of him smiling. Why is that? And while I’m criticizing uptight philosophies, I can’t give a pass to the Stoics, the wisest wet blankets we have. Seneca, the most fun of a stiff bunch, wrote that “The man who laughs at [life], rather than mourns, does more service to the human race.” 5 He’s telling us that humorless people are already partially dead. The very fact that we forget that survival itself is an achievement is funny and absurd. On days when life seems hard, cruel, or pointless, we can try to remember the ridiculously small odds of being alive, and enjoy it, even if the best we can do is find clever ways to complain about our disappointments. Much of the best art and music, works that help us appreciate life, are made by people having a rough time (e.g., most comedians are miserable). Art is their therapy and a gift to us all. But we compulsively take life for granted, justifying this first rule. Even though I love being alive, I don’t wish for immortality. It’s a terrible idea. Kafka wrote, “The meaning of life is that it ends,” and I agree (although he’s a tricky source on how to live, since he was unhappy most of the time 6 [FN 6]). Scary movies are thrilling to watch because the fear of death they evoke helps us to feel alive. Without that fear, without the prospect of it all ending, we’d be more depressed and lost than ever. Death, and the awareness that all things end, creates meaning. For example, if you felt this book was wasting your time, I’d apologize. However, if you were immortal and had the same complaint, I’d feel that you were wasting my time! For an immortal, time would be worthless. For me, every minute lost is irreplaceable. I’d pity you, because I’d know that as an immortal, your life would get increasingly empty as you aged. You’d either endure the endless grief of watching everyone you care about die, or you’d fade into an emotionless zombie who cared about nothing. If we all lived forever, we’d be more selfish and cruel to one another, as death motivates us to care about consequences. I don’t believe in an afterlife either: it’s just too convenient and boring (as David Byrne wrote, “It’s a place where nothing happens” 7 . Even if I did believe in it, I’d think it was a bad idea, as it’s just another flavor of immortality. Instead, I look to nature. In the old-growth forests of the world, when the most majestic trees fall and die, they become nurse logs, helping new trees grow and find their own light. But if those trees never fell, they’d selfishly take up space and resources without offering anything in return. If you wanted to nitpick, you could say the rule should be don’t die, yet . That’s fine. Nitpicking is a sign you’re reading more thoughtfully than dead people do. Well done. Another way to put this is that the denial of death is the denial of life. Millions of people struggle to enjoy a single hour of their day, yet they obsess about living longer instead of better. Or wiser. They just want MORE. We live longer than ever but are probably more miserable than ever too. And as we get more, and get better at counting it, we forget to value what it’s all for. This explains why rich people often have terrible taste. It’s like the sad businessman from The Little Prince , who owned most of the stars in the sky but never loved them. 8 Why? In his obsession to own them all, he forgot to notice, not even once, the wonder of how they shined. We love our dogs and cats because they enjoy life without extensive resumes or worn-out passports. They don’t care about careers, impressing their neighbors, or finding their purpose. Dogs are particularly worthy for their Sisyphus-defying ability to delight in the repetitions of life, thrilled every single time we come home or they get to go outside to chase a ball. Their enthusiasm for life is unparalleled. We admire children for being present in every moment without having to first listen to wellness podcasts or fly to Mexico for ayahuasca yoga retreats. The first question of wisdom to ask then is: why do all living things seem to know how to live well except us? Why does being a person, the supposed pinnacle of evolutionary achievement, often feel like a fight for happiness against the universe? Alan Watts, the legendary, self-described philosophical entertainer, once wrote: The meaning of life is just to be alive. It is so plain and so obvious and so simple. And yet, everybody rushes around in a great panic as if it were necessary to achieve something beyond themselves. 9 Where does this panic we feel come from? This is explained by the second rule. 2. Wake Up One of the worst days of my life was the day I graduated from college. After years of sacrifice and hard work, I had no job, no friends, and no prospects. All my classmates, including my Pittsburgh housemates, Ben, Ed, and Jeff, had flown away. They left to start careers, chase dreams, or spend their summer with family. My parents had just driven away to return to NYC, leaving me alone, with no one to celebrate with on that hot, humid night. As the sun set, I stood on the balcony of my empty apartment, drinking cheap whiskey by myself, looking longingly at the Carnegie Mellon campus. I struggled to accept that I was no longer a student there. I felt alone in a way I had never felt before. For hours, I mindlessly watched cars drive by my street. It seemed that everyone had somewhere to go except for me. As the sky darkened, I struggled to understand why it felt that the earth had fallen away beneath my feet. I was too ashamed to talk to anyone about it. I was in shock at discovering how empty life could feel. I had followed life’s rules, yet somehow here I was. The panic Watts describes is easy to explain: it’s the fear of not meeting the expectations of other people. I suffered that day because I had worked hard to ensure that graduation would be the beginning of my real life. When we are young, we are told that being real is something we earn. We have to find an impressive career or a meaningful purpose with sufficient social status. To go home to live with my parents again meant, at least in my mind, I had lost the game of life. And standing on that balcony, I felt like a loser. There are many flawed stories we believe about ourselves when we are young, and many people never outgrow them. Author Tara Brach calls this the trance of unworthiness, and we need help to snap out of it. 10 Many religions tell us that we are born flawed from the start and will be damned to burn in hell, for eternity, if we don’t fix ourselves. How crazy is that? It would be too cruel to treat puppies or kittens that way, yet we do it to our own young. In Japan, it’s illegal for parents to threaten children with sayings like, “You will go to hell.” 11 They consider it a form of abuse. Deep in our culture, there’s a system of fear that tells us we’re always behind. 12 We’re constantly told we should be smarter, prettier, wealthier, and more productive. But we aren’t given trustworthy maps or reliable guides to achieve those things, so who wouldn’t feel panic? Or feel that they don’t belong? We judge beach bums and the homeless for “doing so little,” for failing to achieve in a capitalistic sense, but isn’t that better than the people we applaud for being productive and successful by hurting the world? Obviously, I did not die in that hospital bed or on my graduation day 30 years ago. Between then and now, I’ve had a great life. But I needed to wake up. I needed to feel Watts’ panic and then deconstruct it. It wasn’t until weeks after my college graduation that I realized I simply needed to start over. And to see that, despite feeling that the world had ended, it actually had not, only my illusions of it had. I was actually quite privileged to go to college at all. So what if I didn’t have a job? So what if I was alone? So what if I had college debt? So what, so what, SO WHAT? I was breathing and my heart was beating. I had fallen asleep in my life, a bad dream of unrealistic pressures, but now I was awake. Earlier, I told you this day was one of the worst of my young life, but it would also turn out to be one of the best. In time, I discovered more about life and myself than I ever had before because of that experience. I was forced to question what was driving me to work so hard, and if it was serving me or someone else. And there was no other way I could learn it. Feeling like a failure opened my eyes. They might have never opened so wide otherwise. If they hadn’t, I doubt that any of my books would exist or that you’d know my name. Seneca wrote long ago that without misfortune, “[you can never] know what you are capable of,” and I know this to be true. Waking up is the second rule in this book because it’s so tricky to follow. We may claim we want to wake up, but when given the choice, we stay in our delusions. We like our comfort zones. Awakening often requires something unexpected, a tragedy or shock, where we’re forced out of our slumber. The Jesuit priest, Anthony de Mello, wrote that many of us are born, live, marry, breed, and die without waking up or even knowing we slept through the whole thing. 13 Here’s a related story: at my gym, there’s a scale in the locker room. I often see men, wearing only a towel, step on the scale to check their weight. They look down at the number and frown in disappointment. Then they step off the scale, take off the towel, and step back on! What are they doing? They are staying asleep. We all have little lies we tell ourselves. We say we want one thing and then we do something else. When we stay asleep, if there is something we don’t like, there is always someone to blame: a parent, a teacher, a boss, or a system. Waking up means you look inside yourself with your eyes open. You finally say: here I am, this is what I am truly like, and here is what is really happening. Alan Watts also said, “You’re under no obligation to be the same person you were five minutes ago.” That is what a person who is awake can say to themselves. The past is only in your mind, and only you can let it go. We often lament our regrets, chastising ourselves by saying, “What was I thinking?” When instead we can say, “Now I am awake. I know more. What action do I want to take now?” Maybe there was no other way to learn the lesson. Be glad you learned it at all. You are awake and can grow from the past instead of being a zombie. Awake people have more choices, and more ways to live well, than those who stay asleep. Waking up can be fun too. Remember your first orgasm. Who knew a body could feel like that! Or the first time you had a vanilla milkshake or chicken tikka masala. Or when you read a book, heard a song, looked at a painting, or saw a movie that opened your mind so wide that you realized the world was inviting you to a lifetime of discoveries. When you are bored or depressed, it may mean you have fallen asleep in ways you didn’t realize. WAKE UP. Wake up, wake up, wake up. Our sad friend Kafka once wrote to a friend that “a book must be the axe for the frozen sea within us.” 14 Breaking that ice is one way to think of waking up. And it’s when that ice is shattered that we transform. Our fears grow in the dark under that ice, and we work hard to bury those fears. The musician Aimee Mann said, “Of the strategies for keeping safe, denial is the least effective…people spend enormous energy keeping things hidden.” That ice gets heavy and weighs us down. And by the time we try to face what’s underneath, those feelings are powerful and sharp enough to cut us to the bone. Rumi wrote, “The cure for the pain is in the pain.” All of the avoidance we do, over years, is far more painful than just feeling the feeling we’re afraid of in that moment and getting through it. But there is good news. When we use that axe, and are brave enough to accept what we find underneath, we can be free to live the life we desire. Buddhist nun and writer Pema Chödrön tells us we should approach our frozen seas with warmth rather than violence. 15 After all, we put that ice there out of self-love, to protect ourselves, even if it has become more of a prison than a sanctuary. With warmth and humor, over time, the ice will melt and crack on its own, allowing us to move through it with grace. It helps to remember that the comfort zone we are in now was once a place we feared. 3: You Are Not Your Thoughts I’ve studied philosophy most of my life, and I’ve often wondered what it would be like to lose my mind or have the mind of someone else. Haven’t you? And as they say, like the Greek myth of King Midas, be careful what you wish for. As the Covid pandemic was winding down in 2021, my right vocal cord was accidentally paralyzed during neck surgery. I could only speak in a quiet, raspy voice. title: #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2)
description: nas edições anteriores #303 | Marcas multiespécie #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ Este não é um manifesto anti-offline. De maneira alguma. A gente não deve desistir de materializar as nossas marcas ou criar experiências no mundo real (não vamos desistir) . Mas neste processo, é importante entender duas coisas: 1. “Offline é o novo luxo” é uma maneira muito simplista de olhar para essa tendência. Ela é indiscutivelmente atrativa para as marcas de luxo, que sempre pautaram a sua comunicação na estética e estilos de vida capazes de diferenciar as pessoas. Quando a estética “comum” é cronicamente online, feita por IA e vidrada em uma tela, o luxo busca ilustrações feitas à mão e experiências sensoriais. Mas a necessidade de desconectar vai além da performance e da distinção social. O que torna o “offline” um movimento muito maior que qualquer trend é justamente a sua capacidade de resgatar uma série de aspectos que têm se perdido na vida moderna. A presença, a atenção, o processo, o aprendizado, a conexão com outras pessoas, a dificuldade (e, consequentemente, a resiliência)… E as tantas sensações, rituais e habilidades que só o mundo real proporciona. Objetos físicos, eventos e atividades manuais devem seguir parte da estratégia das marcas. Não para gerar percepção de luxo ou para fazer igual a uma ou outra. Muito menos para criar novos espaços de mídia que “chamam mais atenção”. E sim pela sua capacidade de interromper o scroll infinito, de ser um lembrete da vida que acontece fora das telas, de gerar valor e, quem sabe, até transformação real nas pessoas. O que nos leva ao segundo ponto. _ 2. Quando o offline se torna hype, é preciso fugir do lugar comum Em 2025, fizemos a primeira edição de uma revista impressa. Ela foi a realização de um sonho antigo, e a materialização da Bits to Brands em cores, ilustrações e páginas enviadas para todo o Brasil. Seu projeto editorial foi feito em outubro de 2024, e a sua impressão em dezembro. Na época, as revistas já começavam a despontar como símbolo de nostalgia - mas não dava para imaginar que seria um movimento tão intenso. Desde então, diversas marcas imprimiram revistas - e serviram café, receberam clubes do livro, ofereceram corridas de rua, distribuíram bonés bordados, estamparam câmeras analógicas… Assim, apenas na sua segunda edição, uma revista não é mais surpreendente ou inovadora. Do mesmo jeito que, em 2026, um boné também não é. (Aliás, um boné vira parte de uma coleção que está chegando a 20 unidades por aqui) O valor do offline não vai a lugar nenhum, mas fazer o básico não é mais o suficiente. O desafio é seguir se reinventando no mesmo formato. A boa notícia é que aí mora a diversão. Porque na tentativa de despertar o que há de mais humano em alguém (a presença, o contato, a memória), precisamos ser humanos primeiro . (criativos, sensíveis, curiosos). Fazer mais ou menos do mesmo jeito, mas um pouco diferente. Fazer mais ou menos a mesma coisa, mas fazer também algo novo. Tornar algo uma tradição, investir de fato em um ritual de marca - mas buscar novas formas de encontrar prazer no processo, e encantar as pessoas com o resultado. Uma revista, a gente já tinha feito. Um álbum de figurinhas foi a primeira vez. Vida longa à nossa imaginação e capacidade de reinvenção - bem humanas, e bem brasileiras :) _ A segunda edição da Revista Bits to Brands está no ar. Neste momento, ela está sendo presenteada para clientes e parceiros da Bits. Mas você vai poder garantir a sua. Na próxima edição da newsletter, dia 15/09, traremos todos os detalhes - e o link! Fiquem de olho porque a quantidade é limitada. Até lá, todos os detalhes estão sendo revelados aos poucos no nosso Instagram. :) para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Essa campanha da Hermann Miller é um ótimo exemplo de como transformar um benefício funcional em conceito criativo. Porque uma cadeira de escritório não precisa querer salvar o mundo ou te fazer chorar com um anúncio. Ela é feita para você sentar melhor. E essa mensagem, com a execução certa, fica irresistível. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O primeiro fim de semana do Rock in Rio foi marcado pela chuva - e pelas filas para pegar brindes nas ativações das marcas. Até agora, destacamos: O karaokê gigante do Itaú (por criar uma experiência memorável verdadeiramente integrada ao evento) A collab entre Uber e LATAM (por entenderem que, juntas, elas poderiam chamar mais atenção do que separadas) _ Para ficar de olho: hoje acontece o primeiro evento da Apple com o novo CEO , John Ternus, no comando. A expectativa é pelo celular dobrável da marca - que não oferece novidade, mas busca se destacar por design e performance. _ O Salesforce atualizou a sua identidade visual. title: Feeling ignored? Here’s what to do
description: One of the hardest situations designers face is being ignored . Here’s my advice on how to deal with this situation and make the most of it. When no one listens to your suggestions What happened. Let’s be realistic. If no one ever took your suggestions and you provided no value, you wouldn’t have a paycheck! You’re just feeling that you deserve more influence and respect that you currently have. Why this is hard . Rejection is painful. It can feel like you don’t exist or your thoughts don’t matter. But only you know what you are capable of. It’s understandable that other people can’t fully see your potential. What not to do. Don’t assume it’s all about you. That would be falling into the ego trap , which you do not want to do. Instead, use your curiosity superpower . Subscribe now Be curious about what you are not noticing. Did others get their suggestions rejected too? Maybe you work for someone who defends the status quo as rejects everyone! All decisions are about tradeoffs, and business, engineering, and leadership can all have valid but conflicting opinions. Unless your suggestions incorporate multiple perspectives, you’re leaving it to the decision-maker to balance tradeoffs across the different points of view each job role tends to have. Investigate. Did you make suggestions to the right person? At the right time? Were they in the right mood? A good place to start is to consider that perhaps you don’t understand the problem they’re trying to solve. What is the user experience for the team leader you want to convince? What are their mental models and goals? What are their frustrations? Use your curiosity and creative skills to figure out the right place, time, medium, and style to offer your suggestions so they’re most likely to be effective. What to do next time. What is your relationship with the decision-maker? How much do they trust you? People agree to ideas based on trust more than the merit of the idea itself. So while your ideas might be great, they may not know you well enough to take risk to be on your idea. Trust has to be earned. It’s human nature. What past experience do they have taking your suggestions and having success? Decisions are as much about the relationship as the idea itself. Reach out and ask for feedback on how your suggestions can be more useful next time, instead of focusing on the limitations of your coworkers.

Porque não é uma coincidência que este seja o adjetivo mais utilizado ao lado da palavra “offline”. Tanto porque o “luxo” é mais valioso e raro, quanto porque ele é aquilo que foge do comum. Quando uma estética ou comportamento se torna o básico, aquilo que todo mundo tem, beirando até o “brega” - performar superioridade intelectual e social é se afastar dela. (A relação entre consumo e performance social está super bem explicada em Coisa de Rico , de Michel Alcoforado). Se nos últimos anos o comum é ser hiperconectado, cronicamente online e passar incontáveis horas arrastando para cima imóvel, o que passa a comunicar luxo e status é desconectar. Ler livros de verdade, fazer atividade física ao ar livre, acessórios tecnológicos mais vintage, encontros para discutir temas específicos, o resgate dos hábitos e atividades sociais das avós (do tricô ao nonna-maxxing )… É por essas e outras que a Miu Miu tem um clube do livro, a Bottega Veneta lançou um jogo de Jenga, a Prada fez uma floricultura e as marcas de luxo têm disputado espaço para fazer ativações nos grandes torneios de tênis pelo mundo. O offline se tornou, sim, sinônimo de luxo. Mas não pára por aí. _ O offline se tornou território de desejo das marcas por motivos certos e errados, racionais e abstratos, mas muitos deles ancorados em comportamentos e demandas bem reais. Um deles é a distinção social. Mas ativações no mundo real, eventos, experiências e objetos físicos despertam interesse também porque são comunitários, sensoriais, duráveis, memoráveis e humanos. Cada um desses aspectos parte de demandas da vida contemporânea que começam no excesso de telas, mas se estendem para a ausência de interações sociais, a substituição do corpo físico pela imagem editada de alguém e até o tal “AI Slop”. Num parque a gente não precisa ficar se perguntando se algo é IA ou não a cada dois minutos (ainda). Porque o offline é comunidade , ele nos permite lembrar que não estamos sozinhos nos nossos gostos e hobbies - seja correr uma meia maratona, seja ter sido fã da Xuxa na infância. Porque o offline é sensorial , ele nos lembra que cada um é um corpo, e não apenas um cérebro e as pontas dos dedos. E que um corpo é capaz de sentir gostos, cheiros, toques, de dançar, cantar, esbarrar, ver e ser visto e se relacionar - de verdade. Porque o offline é durável , ele se torna representação no mundo real de quem a gente é. Aquilo que decora os nossos ambientes, que compõe as nossas coleções , que está pendurado nas nossas bolsas e mochilas ou até geladeiras - ajuda a contar a nossa história. Diga-me o que colecionas e te direi quem és. Porque o offline é memorável, ele é uma grande oportunidade para as marcas investirem seus orçamentos de comunicação de forma mais assertiva. Estamos descobrindo que reunir um grupo de pessoas verdadeiramente atentas e interessadas tem mais valor do que atingir milhões de views sabe-se lá de quem. E porque o offline é humano, ele é o único ambiente onde a gente vivencia o tempo de forma linear, a arte de forma artesanal e o mundo conforme a nossa própria curadoria de experiências - e não a de um algortimo. Não é à toa que todo mundo quer mais disso. _ Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . title: What is the speed of your ideas?
description: We’re taught to believe that great ideas get adopted faster, but this really isn’t true. Why? Ideas change things and most people do not like change. People don’t admit this of course, but watch how people behave and you’ll see it. Most of the time people want security and safety and a great idea will create uncertainty before anything else. We could define a truly great idea as one that’s easy to convince people to use, but this often means only our most convenient ideas go anywhere. Why isn’t this common knowledge? Not sure! I wrote a popular book about the myths of innovation and my theory is we all like to believe we’re pioneers and innovators, even when we’re actually as risk-averse as a pile of rocks . Certainly in the business world executives regularly talk about change… and then change nothing. We’re a funny species really. But it’s our job as designers to help the world, so here we are. One simple way to understand all this is what I call idea velocity. What is idea velocity? Idea velocity is a way to measure how fast ideas move through your workplace. Not just your ideas, all ideas . It’s a way to take yourself out of the equation, at least for a moment, to really see where you are. Some organizations move fast. Most move pretty slow. Where are you? It should be the first question you ask before you come up with ideas for anything. Subscribe now For example, lets take a fictional respected international bank called MegaCrunchBank . Banks are among the most conservative workplace cultures for obvious reasons: they are paid to be reliable and secure above all else. The idea velocity at a bank is very slow . It takes years, and often regulations, for things to change. If Tesla or Marie Curie, or the next super genius creative thinker, worked at a bank, no matter how brilliant they were, change would be slow. There would be dozens of meetings and committee discussions just to update the website. Banks have slow idea velocity and this is true no matter how talented a person is or how great their ideas are. Where is idea velocity fast ? A good example is a three person startup company started by friends. Since they trust each other and there is more work to do than people, everyone is empowered to make decisions. If you volunteered to work on the website, you could have almost any ideas for it and just go make them happen. Why? You’re doing the work. It’s that simple. In short, idea velocity is the existing pace for how ideas become decisions . That pace is shaped by culture and not how great your ideas are. So what does this mean? Designers are often unhappy because we are idea people. We always want high idea velocity. The problem is almost no one else does! Organizations are built to survive, not necessarily to change. Most job functions are there to stabilize things, not to change them. This means it’s critical we measure the pace of change where we are. We must be students of which leaders want a faster pace. Which teams are more ambitious. We need to look at the org chart not in terms of hierarchy but in terms of creative pace and receptivity to changing things. This helps make the system work for you, and not against you . Use idea velocity to help you Once you buy the basic theory of idea velocity, there are ways to use it to your advantage. Here are some questions to help: What is the best example of a big idea leading to change where you work? What can you learn from it? What is an example of a respected leader with a big idea failing to get adoption? What can you learn? Who has the power or influence that allows their ideas to move faster? How can you make them an ally? What is the fastest pace you’ve seen in your organization? Why are you expecting your ideas to move any faster? How can you set realistic expectations of the idea velocity of your team, so you don’t get angry or frustrated for something you can not change? Velocity can increase with momentum. You might need a series of small wins to earn the trust for bigger, faster change. Spend the rest of this week thinking about pace of change. It’s a different and more useful lens for people with ideas.

title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. title: leia se você tiver múltiplos interesses ☕️🐢
description: Parte da minha família veio à Espanha para ficar uns dias perto de mim e da minha filhinha. Pra estar mais presente, abri o meu túnel do tempo e escolhi uma edição antiga pela qual tenho muito carinho :¬) Espero que você goste tanto quanto a Eleninha gostou dos desenhos de fruta que fizemos! É possível ser multipotencial, mas finalizar projetos? É possível focar, mas sem deixar a sua natureza curiosa de lado? Depois de aaanos frustrado , aprendi alguns caminhos que me fazem dizer “sim” para as perguntas acima. Nessa edição, queria dividir um deles com você :¬) O ministério da criatividade “a diverte”: isso não é uma fórmula pronta. Cada pessoa e projeto tem um contexto diferente. O texto não contém glúten - mas, como tudo na internet, não é para todo mundo, nem para todo tipo de projeto. Acho bonito pensar em projetos como sementinhas que precisam de diferentes níveis de nutrição. E como essas sementes se alimentam de recursos super valiosos - seu tempo, dinheiro e energia - é muito sensato que a gente cuide deles com carinho. Você já deve ter ouvido 1004 vezes que definir prioridades é importante. Mas se, assim como eu, você também tem múltiplos interesses e ideias, considera fazer isso dessa forma: Transformar em prioridade só aquilo que você poderia sustentar numa semana ruim (uma hipótese inicial que pode ser ajustada, claro). Criar uma linha do tempo e inserir os [1] projetos atuais (prioridades) e [2] projetos futuros. Por que recomendo isso? :¬) Parece bobo: mas isso traz clareza visual sobre onde (e por quanto tempo) você pensa em investir seus recursos. Mas isso NÃO quer dizer que você precisa deixar sua curiosidade de lado e esquecer dos futuros projetos, viu? Não é uma escolha binária. Por que? :¬) Porque, felizmente, o processo criativo é composto por etapas diferentes. Deixar ideias marinando e construir um acervo de referências também é parte do processo criativo, concorda? E o mais legal: Essas partes do processo podem fluir espontaneamente: quando esbarramos com novidades, notamos algo ao redor, fazemos associações aleatórias, etc. E por que isso é lindo? Isso permite nutrir as sementes do futuro com leveza - sem desviar seus recursos das prioridades que você definiu. Nem tudo é 8 ou 80. Nem tudo é preto ou branco. Um jardim cresce com ritmos diferentes. “E, na prática… o que você faz, Tiagão? Gosto do Bulbassauro, mas chega de analogia com planta.” Projetos atuais: transformar em hábitos. Algo sustentável, que cabe na sua rotina. Esse vídeo ajuda com isso. Futuros projetos: ir salvando referências, anotações e links em pastinhas separadas; em algum momento, você-do-futuro vai transformá-las em prioridade :¬) Começar algo novo = um prêmio. E, agora, você começa com a confiança de que aprendeu a usar o ponto final. E, por último, mas não menos importante: É essencial – e uso essa palavra com muita intenção – lembrar que: As ideias-que-você-ainda-não- começou vão parecer “perfeitas” na sua imaginação… até você botar a mão na massa. É na hora da fazeção que a gente encontra os desconfortos, desafios e as imperfeições. Esse constraste faz a gente desistir de ideias, mesmo que ainda fizesse sentido terminá-las. Por isso, sugiro se preparar (antes!) para o inevitável canto das sereias. P.S. Se esse texto ajudar UM ser vivo do Sistema Solar, eu já fico feliz. P.P.S. Já me frustrei (muito!) por achar que focar = ignorar a minha natureza curiosa e multipotencial. Por isso, torço para que você vá nutrindo o seu jardim e, aos pouquinhos, comece a tirar as suas ideias do papel :¬) 🥕 o melhor bolo de cenoura era o da minha avó. 🎾 uma curadoria de joguinhos para substituir redes sociais. 🌍 um jogo divertido para aprender sobre a geografia da África. 👀 eu queria tanto ter criado isso aqui. 🐦 curti as brisas visuais do Adam. Esse é um pum sobre assinaturas. Estou num momento de questionar o que assino ( streaming , apps , etc.) para cancelar ou inserir coisas novas. Como você e muita gente que lê a news podem curtir assuntos parecidos, queria te perguntar: Quais das suas assinaturas valem muuuito a pena no seu contexto? Aquela que você paga, com prazer, todo mês ou todo ano? Por que? :¬) Deixe um comentário Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

title: sua geladeira ☕️🐢
description: A gente cozinha com os ingredientes que estão na nossa geladeira. “Ai, ai, ai… Lá vem o Tiago com outra analogia que envolve comida....” Mas falando sério: isso não rima com o processo criativo? Pensa só: os ingredientes são o nosso repertório e a geladeira é a nossa cachola :¬) Ou seja, guardamos as referências e vivências de forma intencional (ou subconsciente) por lá. Um dos maiores desafios de seres humanos que habitam o Sistema Solar em 2026 é não deixar que os algoritmos das redes sociais sempre façam as compras. Afinal, a rotina é corrida! Deixá-los escolher por nós deixa tudo tão fácil e conveniente , não é? Eles já sabem do que a gente gosta. É só se deixar levar. Não precisa pensar ou gastar energia pra consumir. E como toda “bolha” tem ingredientes parecidos, a gente acaba provando uma variedade pequena de pratos. [ esse brinquedo de comidinhas de madeira é da Elena - e é muuuito divertido! ] Mudar o nosso consumo impacta diretamente no que a gente pensa, sente e cria. O processo criativo não começa na cozinha: ele envolve a escolha do mercado, o tempo que ficamos nele e os ingredientes novos que a gente escolhe experimentar :¬) garimpos 🦭 eu e você já temos conexão pelo LinkedIn ? :) 🐬 mais uma curadoria de músicas de fases aquáticas de videogame. 💧 falando em água: essa instalação artística é tão simples, mas tão legal. 🐙 se você curte branding, criatividade e desconfia de quem fala sobre o “jeito certo” de fazer as coisas, acho que você vai curtir esse livro. pum Esse pum é um eco do texto ali de cima :¬) Tenho brisado muito sobre o quanto cada pessoa que sigo me inspira a [1] comprar coisas ou a [2] criar coisas. As pessoas que mais te inspiram têm feito você querer criar mais ou comprar mais? E, pra você, qual é o limite saudável entre esses dois? P.S. Lembrando que não é um papo binário e com resposta de múltipla escolha - é só um convite pra gente pausar e pensar :¬) Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

title: Why CEOs ignore design leaders
description: Designers have big egos. There, I said it. An ego is a sense of self, and creative people need strong ones to have faith in their ideas. But ego is dangerous and can get in the way of just about everything else. I chose to make the first part of Why Design Is Hard directly about the designer ego trap , and how blind designers are to our self-defeating behavior. We spend too much time with other designers who have similiar egos and personalities which means we’ve spent decades sharing our complaints into an echo chamber of learned helplessness. The reason CEOs ignore design leaders is simple: CEOs ignore almost everyone . That’s their job. Can you imagine what their schedule looks like? VPs ignore almost everyone too. Why? The entire organization is competing for their attention. Every person in every job has their own agenda and wants to influence the VP to get it. To be a good executive means intentionally limiting who can influence you and how they can do it. If you feel ignored, here is the best advice: be curious, not judgmental. Judgement keeps you where you are but complaints alone are not effective arguments . Remember that curiosity is your superpower as a designer and it will find you a way forward. You are being judgmental and egocentric if you say: My CEO is an idiot (even if it’s true, so what? This can be an advantage) Why I am not involved more? Why do they hate designers? Why do they dislike me personally? Why don’t THEY get it ? Why I am an always on the outside? These are all EGO centered questions. These questions are entirely centered on YOU. And it’s no surprise that when you raise complaints like this you are probably seen as being self-involved. CEOs hear selfish complaints all day long from directors and other executives and it’s exhausting. As much as you’re rightfully frustrated, much of your peer group in other roles are frustrated too and voicing similiar complaints for more power. No department head shows up and says “Hey CEO! Cut my team in half please. We’re just not that important.” They are always demanding something. CEOs and VPs tune out much of the complaining as static. They have to. Design culture has normalized the belief that these complaints have any effect and it’s a terrible mistake. To be more effective you must act on curiosity and instead ask: Maybe there are good reasons great design is not a strategy where I work ? If I’m left out, who is on the inside and how did they get there? What can I learn? How can I partner with them? What is a better promise I can make to solve important problems for powerful people? What do I not understand about how things really get done where I work? What am I willing to change in myself to have more influence without my workplace changing? Or what do I need to accept about the limits of my role ? One major hypocrisy of designers is we claim superiority at understand people, but then fail to study our own coworkers to better understand them. We just let our egos focus on blame instead, which leads nowhere . The above list is simple, actionable questions, but design culture does not embrace them yet. Good questions lead to discoveries. Simply by reaching out to people with curiosity you will get more useful responses. For example, to say “Hey Sally, as the VP of engineering, I can help your team be more efficient, but I’m not involved early enough to help. What advice do you have for me?” Is a request for involvement combined with an offer to help solve a problem. This will always be more effective than demanding involvement in anything because of your job title (which designers have a long history of doing). Subscribe now But these ego habits are hard to shake . The response this book and the dozens of talks I’ve given on it is often, “why should I have to do this?” And my answer is you don’t! But if you are miserable it is you who has to change something. No one is going to do it for you. It could be to accept how organizations tend to work and stop dreaming of design nirvana. It might be realizing you are competing for influence with powerful people and it’s a skill to learn. Or perhaps it’s to reevaluate where you expect creative satisfaction to come from and seek it somewhere outside of your job. But all three require moving past the limitations of ego and to open your eyes. title: #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026
description: nas edições anteriores #299 | Nesta Copa do Mundo, olhe em volta #300 | A vida das coisas tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Às vésperas da Copa do Mundo, em 2022, comentamos na edição 188 que era a primeira Copa pós-TikTok e a primeira Copa pós-Casimiro. O que mudou o jeito de transmitir, de assistir, de anunciar e até de se relacionar com o evento. Quatro anos depois, a Copa de 2026 trouxe outras primeiras vezes, que certamente vão criar novas dinâmicas para marcas, fãs e espectadores. Essa é a primeira Copa pós-inteligência artificial generativa. O que se refletiu em feeds lotados de conteúdo em tempo real durante os jogos (a CazéTV, por exemplo, soltou dezenas de posts sobre o Cristiano Ronaldo em minutos), e deepfakes de jogadores em situações inusitadas. Um ponto de atenção aqui é ver uma tecnologia tão potencialmente perigosa se tornar apenas engraçada quando utilizada, por exemplo, para recriar uma cena de As Branquelas com Vini Jr. e Erling Haaland. A Copa do Mundo parece ser a sua virada definitiva - de uso indevido de imagem e fábrica de fake news a… fábrica de memes. _ Essa é a primeira Copa pós-proliferação das bets. E o momento, que parecia ideal para sua consolidação definitiva e ganho de credibilidade, teve efeito contrário. As marcas de bet se tornaram tóxicas para as transmissões que patrocinaram, atrapalhando a experiência dos espectadores e gerando antipatia a todos os envolvidos. O canal, o narrador, a marca, até os jogadores. E é além de entretenimento. 61% das apostas sugeridas pela CazéTV foram perdidas. Isso sem contar na Virgínia, influenciadora não-oficial do evento, sugerindo que seus seguidores apostassem em uma improvável vitória de Cabo Verde. Enquanto essas plataformas perdem de vista os "zeros” do quanto faturam em uma Copa do Mundo, cada aposta é dinheiro real de milhões de brasileiros, que impacta na sua renda, qualidade de vida, estrutura familiar e saúde mental. Neste momento, ainda está aberto um território para marcas que quiserem se posicionar abertamente contra as bets. De todos os lugares possíveis para assistir a uma grande partida de futebol, será que os segundos de delay contariam mais do que uma transmissão livre de gatilhos para apostar? _ Essa é a primeira Copa pós-tradução automática. Eis um novo universo de interação e entretenimento na internet: a tradução automática de posts na timeline do Twitter (X). Colocada no ar em março de 2026, bem a tempo. Basicamente, essa feature faz com que tweets escritos em qualquer idioma apareçam na sua timeline em português. Existe uma sinalização discreta da tradução, mas a experiência é fluida - você passa por aquele comentário como se ele estivesse realmente no seu contexto. E contexto é chave aqui, porque agora quem fala pode ser compreendido em toda a sua espontaneidade, sem precisar adaptar as suas palavras a quem ouve. Como naquele episódio clássico de Modern Family, em que a personagem de Sofia Vergara, uma mulher latina, se frustra com o marido americano porque não consegue transmitir toda a sua personalidade em inglês. “Você sabe o quão frustrante é ter que traduzir tudo na minha cabeça antes de falar? Você sabe o quão inteligente eu sou em espanhol?” Todo mundo que já tentou se comunicar em um outro idioma entende o que ela quer dizer. Nós somos naturalmente mais espontâneos onde temos mais fluência. Voltando ao Twitter (X), é justamente a espontaneidade e a total fluência do brasileiro em memes que agora começam a se espalhar pelo mundo - um post traduzido de cada vez. Nesta Copa do Mundo, um francês e um brasileiro puderam discutir como se estivessem na mesma mesa de bar, se entendendo plenamente. E bom… se ofendendo, também. Nessa Torre de Babel às avessas, a comunicação plena entre culturas encontrou no futebol um território comum para ser exercitada. “A minha parte favorita da Copa do Mundo tem sido acompanhar os brasileiros acabarem com os outros países, um por um, nesse aplicativo… Toda vez que eu vejo um tweet “traduzido do português” eu sei que vai ser a coisa mais sensacional, sem limites e precisa que eu já vi" Cronicamente online, extremamente criativo e ocasionalmente sem limites, o nosso senso de humor ganhou o mundo e ditou vários memes da Copa - agora globalmente. Com destaque para a rixa imaginária entre o técnico Ancelotti e Endrick, que foi ganhando forma nas situações mais absurdas. Isso viralizou a ponto de uma marca europeia entrar na conversa. O que inaugura uma nova era de interação nas redes sociais: o seu social listening agora é global. Porque o Twitter é só o começo. Todas as redes sociais já vêm testando suas versões de tradução automática, e até dublagem de vídeos.
